svg.title: Unicast forwards on the destination, multicast forwards on a reverse check of the source
svg.desc: Two panels. Left: unicast looks up the destination in the FIB, takes the longest match and forwards out that interface, whatever the ingress port was. Right: multicast reads the source address, looks up the route back to that source, and compares it with the ingress interface; only an exact match forwards into the outgoing interface list. A bottom band lists the three causes of RPF failure - asymmetric unicast and multicast paths, ECMP, and a BGP next hop that is unreachable - and notes that the failure is silent.
svg.text: The lookup is inverted
Unicast asks "where is the destination". Multicast asks "did this packet arrive the way back to its source".
UNICAST
Decide on the destination address
packet arrives
on any link
lookup dst in FIB
longest match
forward out
that interface
The ingress interface is irrelevant. The same packet arriving
on a "wrong" link is still forwarded, and the network has no
way to notice a forwarding loop created by policy.
Loop protection is a different mechanism: TTL, uRPF.
Neither of them builds or constrains a distribution tree.
The forwarding state is per prefix, independent of who is receiving.
MULTICAST
Decide on the source address, at the ingress
packet in
route back to
ingress == Gi0/1 ?
yes: forward to OIL
The check happens once, on the way in. The outgoing interface
list is built by joins, not by the destination address.
A mismatch drops the packet with no ICMP, no log, no counter
except the drop counter on the interface.
show ip rpf 10.1.1.10 -> RPF interface, RPF neighbour, RPF type
RPF type tells you where the answer came from: unicast, static, mbgp, mtrie.
WHY THE CHECK FAILS, AND WHY YOU DO NOT HEAR ABOUT IT
1. Asymmetric path
Unicast prefers A, multicast arrives on B.
Fix the metric, or pin a static mroute.
2. ECMP
The return route has two equal paths and the
chosen one is not the ingress. ip multicast multipath
hashes on the source, so one source still uses one path.
3. iBGP next hop
The BGP route is best but its next hop is not
reachable: next-hop-self, or a static mroute.
The silent part
No ICMP unreachable, no syslog, no retransmission.
Only show ip mroute count and a packet capture
prove the drop, which is why RPF comes first in every runbook.
Never debug the receiver first.
Ask where the packet entered, then ask
where the route to the source points.
Static mroute outranks every other
source: a leftover from last year's
migration is the classic trap.
